title: Usama ibn Munqidh's memoirs
hookLine: a Syrian knight's memoir of the Crusades, curious and human
tomorrow: a sick poet, a dream, a cloak. what did he write when he woke?

lines: THE WAR AS MAPS AND ARROWS.
A KNIGHT WHO FOUGHT THE FRANKS.
cards: On the news, a war usually arrives as maps, arrows and one word for the other side. Here's a memoir that doesn't fit that. Usama ibn Munqidh was a Syrian knight who fought the Franks, the Crusaders, for much of his life.

Yet in his memoir there's an odd line. When he visits Jerusalem, he describes the Templars, the Frankish knights then holding the al-Aqsa mosque, as his friends. They give him a small place beside it to pray.
A knight on one side, calling knights on the other side friends. How does that fit?

teach.b: Keep reading and the scene answers it. Usama stands to pray, and a Frank he doesn't know rushes in, grabs him and turns him to face east: this is how you pray.

The Templars pull the man away and apologize. He's a stranger, they explain, just arrived from the Frankish lands, and he's never seen anyone pray any other way. Usama turns back and finishes his prayer.
Then he writes the moral he drew: the Franks who had lived a while among Muslims behaved better than the newcomers. That's the key to the puzzle.

Usama doesn't see an army; he sees people, one at a time. Some he likes, some he mocks, some he can't figure out, and he writes all of them down with a traveler's curiosity. He never stops being on his own side.
But his memoir's name, the Book of Learning by Example, tells you what he's after: lessons, not scores.

He also writes, as a man who survived many battles, that a life's length is in God's hands: boldness doesn't shorten it, and caution doesn't stretch it. War, for him, is still a place where humans meet.
That's a human view of war.

how: Readers today study Usama ibn Munqidh's memoir as a window on the Crusade years from a Muslim knight's side; teachers use it to show enemies seen as people, curious and complicated.

games.q: what does “usama ibn munqidh's memoirs” mean?
o: a chronicle of battles written for a sultan's court
a Syrian knight's book about friends and foes in the Crusades
a Crusader's diary of his years ruling a Syrian town

games.q: the knight's memoir — tap the pairs.
p: a Syrian knight who wrote a memoir
gave him a place to pray

s: in the Crusade years, Muslims and Franks never had a friendly word
Usama calls some Templars his friends, and they apologize when a newcomer bothers him at prayer.
Usama says the Franks who'd lived among Muslims behaved better than newcomers
that's the moral he draws from the scene at al-Aqsa.
a human view of war means Usama switched sides
he never stops being on his own side. he just sees people, one at a time.

games.q: your school plays its biggest rival. one of their players helps your injured teammate off the field. at the team dinner, everyone trashes their whole school. what fits Usama's memoir?
o: join in. loyalty means you don't praise the other side.
tell the story of that player by name, rivalry and all.
say the rivalry is pointless and you're done with it.
games.why: Usama keeps his side and still writes down the decent people on the other one, by name and by deed.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind someone you mostly know as the other side: a rival team, a neighbor you argue with, a cousin on the far end of every debate.
Find one ordinary, human thing about them, the way they laugh, someone they look after. Stay with that one detail.

wordCard.voice: Usama ibn Munqidh's memoirs: a Syrian knight's book of the Crusade years, full of curious, frank portraits of friend and foe.

orig.note: Arabic: i'tibar, taking a lesson from what happens; the word in the memoir's name.

carryVoice: Something for the road: a human view of war, where even across a battle line a face stays a face. Travelers and historians, all eight, complete.

sources.ref: Usama ibn Munqidh, Kitab al-I'tibar: the visit to Jerusalem, the Templars ('my friends'), the newly arrived Frank who turned him east, and the moral about newcomers
Usama ibn Munqidh, Kitab al-I'tibar: a life's term is decreed; boldness does not shorten it nor caution lengthen it
